summary: Describes how to build point-to-multipoint label switched paths that span several routing areas. The path is split into segments inside each area, and BGP is used to stitch the segments together between areas. This keeps the per-area routing protocols independent while still delivering multicast-style traffic across a large network.

plainLanguage.summary: This document explains how to build a one-to-many MPLS tunnel that crosses several routing areas inside one operator's network. The tunnel is cut into pieces, one per area, and BGP carries the information that tells the routers how the pieces fit together.

subtitle: How a multicast tunnel is built across several routing areas by stitching area-local segments together with BGP.

tldr.problem: A provider that runs several IGP areas inside one autonomous system still wants one multicast tunnel from a sending edge router to every receiving edge router, but each area's routing protocol knows nothing about the other areas.
tldr.mechanism: The document splits the service tunnel into an ingress area segment, a backbone area segment and an egress area segment, and uses BGP between the areas to carry the signalling that stitches them together.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard from May 2015, updated by RFC 8534, and it is the standard way to run point-to-multipoint MPLS tunnels across IGP area boundaries.

facts.label: Segments per service LSP
facts.value: Three: ingress area, backbone area, egress area

today: RFC 7524 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2015. It is updated by RFC 8534 and has not been obsoleted, so it remains the standard description of inter-area point-to-multipoint segmented LSPs.

sections.title: Multicast Tunnels Across Areas
sections.content:
The document describes procedures for building inter-area point-to-multipoint segmented service LSPs by partitioning such LSPs into intra-area segments and using BGP as the inter-area routing and label distribution protocol. Within each IGP area, the intra-area segments are either carried over intra-area P2MP LSPs, potentially using P2MP LSP hierarchy, or instantiated using ingress replication. The intra-area P2MP LSPs may be signalled with P2MP RSVP-TE (RFC 4875) or P2MP mLDP (RFC 6388). Where ingress replication is used in an IGP area, multipoint-to-point LDP LSPs (RFC 5036) or point-to-point RSVP-TE LSPs (RFC 3209) may be used within the area. The applications that use these inter-area service LSPs may be BGP Multicast VPN, VPLS multicast, or global table multicast over MPLS.

The primary use case is when the Provider Edge routers are in different areas but in the same autonomous system, and thousands or more PEs need P2MP connectivity. That may be the case when MPLS is pushed further to the metro edge and the metros sit in different IGP areas, or when a service provider's network has multiple IGP areas in a single AS with a large number of PEs. Seamless MPLS is the industry term for that situation, so one of the applicabilities of this document is that it describes the multicast procedures for seamless MPLS.

Two other documents, RFC 6514 and RFC 7117, already specify procedures for building segmented inter-AS P2MP service LSPs. This document complements them by extending the segmented P2MP LSP model so that it also applies to inter-area service LSPs; an inter-AS deployment could use the inter-AS segmented P2MP LSPs of those documents with each intra-AS segment built using the inter-area segmented P2MP LSPs described here.
sections.plainLanguage: Large networks are split into areas so that each area's routing protocol stays simple. But a multicast tunnel still has to reach every area. This document works out how to join the pieces back together.

sections.title: How the Service Tunnel Is Split
sections.content:
Within an AS, a P2MP service LSP is partitioned into three segments: the ingress area segment, the backbone area segment and the egress area segment. Within each area a segment is carried over an intra-area P2MP LSP or instantiated using ingress replication. When intra-area P2MP LSPs are used, there can be either a one-to-one or a many-to-one mapping between intra-area segments and a given intra-area P2MP LSP, the latter using P2MP LSP hierarchy with upstream-assigned labels. For simplicity of presentation the document assumes P2MP LSP hierarchy is used even with a one-to-one mapping, in which case an Implicit NULL is used as the upstream-assigned label. When intra-area segments are instantiated using ingress replication, multiple such segments may be carried in the same P2P RSVP-TE or MP2P LDP LSP, which can be achieved using downstream-assigned labels alone.

The ingress area segment of a P2MP service LSP is rooted at a PE, or at an ASBR in the case where the service LSP spans multiple ASes. Its leaves are other PEs, ASBRs and ABRs in the same area as the root PE. The backbone area segment is rooted at either an ABR connected to the ingress area, an ASBR if the ASBR is present in the backbone area, or a PE if the PE is present in the backbone area. Its leaves are the ABRs connected to the egress areas, PEs in the backbone area, or ASBRs in the backbone area. The egress area segment is rooted at an ABR in the egress area, and its leaves are the PEs and ASBR in that egress area, the latter covering the case where the service LSP spans multiple ASes. For a given P2MP service LSP there may be more than one backbone segment, each rooted at its own ingress ABR, and more than one egress area segment, each rooted at its own egress ABR.

The document uses the term A-D routes for auto-discovery routes, and an implementation that supports the document MUST implement the procedures in the following sections.
sections.plainLanguage: One long tunnel becomes three shorter ones: the part near the sender, the part crossing the backbone, and the part near the receivers. Each is built and signalled by the routers in its own area.

sections.title: The Extended Community That Marks the Route
sections.content:
The document defines a new Transitive IPv4-Address-Specific Extended Community sub-type named Inter-Area P2MP Next-Hop, and a new BGP Transitive IPv6-Address-Specific Extended Community sub-type with the same name. A PE, an ABR or an ASBR constructs the community as follows. The Global Administrator field MUST be set to an IP address of the PE, ABR or ASBR that originates or advertises the route carrying it, for example the loopback address. The Local Administrator field MUST be set to 0. If the Global Administrator field is an IPv4 address the IPv4-Address-Specific Extended Community is used, and if it is an IPv6 address the IPv6-Address-Specific one is used.

When BGP MVPN I-PMSI or S-PMSI A-D routes, or VPLS A-D routes, are advertised or propagated to signal inter-area P2MP service LSPs, to indicate that these LSPs should be segmented using the procedures of the document, the routes MUST carry this extended community. It MUST be included by the PE that originates the route, or by an ASBR that re-advertises the route into its own AS, with the Global Administrator field set to the advertising PE or ASBR's IP address. ABRs MUST also include it as they re-advertise such routes, setting the Global Administrator field to their own IP address. Its presence tells ABRs and PEs or ASBRs that they have to follow the procedures of this document where those differ from those of RFC 6514 or RFC 7117.

An ASBR that receives from an IBGP peer a route carrying the community SHOULD remove it before re-advertising to an EBGP peer. If an ASBR receives such a route from an EBGP peer and the inter-area P2MP service LSP it signals should not be segmented, the ASBR MUST remove the community before re-advertising to its IBGP peers.
sections.plainLanguage: One extra field on the route says "treat this as an inter-area segmented tunnel". Each router that re-advertises the route puts its own address in it, so the chain of routers is visible.

sections.title: Learning the Multicast Group
sections.content:
Each inter-area P2MP service LSP has a P2MP Forwarding Equivalence Class associated with it, and the egress PEs need to learn that FEC in order to start building the egress area segment. The FEC is learned either by configuration or through the application-specific procedures, such as the MVPN or VPLS procedures.

For BGP MVPN, egress PEs and ASBRs discover the FEC of the service LSPs using the Inclusive Provider Multicast Service Interface or Selective PMSI A-D routes originated by the ingress PEs or ASBRs, with the modifications described in the document. The NLRI of such routes encodes the P2MP FEC. The procedures require that at least one ABR in a given IGP area act as a Route Reflector for MVPN A-D routes, responsible for re-advertising them across area boundaries. Such a Route Reflector may also re-advertise routes within the same area, in which case it follows the plain BGP Route Reflector procedures of RFC 4456.

The Leaf Information Required flag MUST be set in the PMSI Tunnel attribute of the MVPN A-D routes when they are originated by the ingress PEs or ASBRs, except where a matter of policy there is no aggregation of ingress area segments and mLDP is used to establish the intra-area transport LSPs in the ingress area. The same requirement applies when an ingress ABR or an egress ABR re-advertises the routes, with the exception stated in terms of backbone area or egress area segments respectively. These procedures apply whether the intra-area segments are realised by intra-area P2MP LSPs or by ingress replication.

For VPLS, egress PEs discover the FEC of the service LSPs using the VPLS A-D routes or VPLS S-PMSI A-D routes originated by the ingress PEs, with the NLRI again encoding the FEC. The same Leaf Information Required rule applies, and the routes must carry the Inter-Area P2MP Segmented Next-Hop extended community. At least one ABR in a given area must act as a Route Reflector for VPLS A-D routes, and when re-advertising them a Route Reflector MUST NOT modify the BGP Next Hop.

For global table multicast, an egress PE learns the (S/*,G) of a multicast stream as a result of receiving IGMP or PIM messages on one of its IP multicast interfaces, and that forms the P2MP FEC. For each such FEC there MAY exist a distinct inter-area P2MP service LSP, or multiple FECs MAY be carried over a single one.
sections.plainLanguage: Each receiving router works out which multicast group it wants and tells the network about it, using the same auto-discovery routes the application already uses, plus the new marker field.

sections.title: What the Egress Edge Router Signals
sections.content:
The egress PE first determines the upstream node it should use, and then originates a Leaf A-D route that asks for the traffic to be delivered to it. When ingress replication is used to instantiate the egress area segment, the Leaf A-D route MUST carry a downstream-assigned label in the PMSI Tunnel attribute, where the PMSI Tunnel Type is set to ingress replication, and a PE MUST assign a distinct MPLS label for each Leaf A-D route it originates.

The Next Hop field of the route's MP_REACH_NLRI attribute SHOULD be set to the same IP address as the one carried in the Originating Router's IP Address field of the route. To constrain the distribution of the route, the originating PE constructs an IP-based Route Target Extended Community by placing the IP address of the upstream node in the Global Administrator field, with the Local Administrator field set to 0, and adds it to the Leaf A-D route. The PE then advertises the route to the upstream node.

For global table multicast there are two options. The first does not carry IP multicast shared trees over the MPLS network, so when an egress PE creates (*,G) state as a result of receiving PIM or IGMP messages, it does not propagate that state using Leaf A-D routes. Whenever a Rendezvous Point co-located with a PE discovers a new multicast source, or a PE that is not configured as an RP discovers one from MSDP messages, the RP or PE SHOULD originate a BGP Source Active A-D route, whose NLRI carries a route distinguisher of 0, the source and the group, and whose route target is an AS-specific one with the Global Administrator field set to the AS of the advertising router. The route SHOULD carry the NO_EXPORT community so that it stays within that AS. The second option does carry shared trees over the MPLS network, so the egress PE propagates its (*,G) state using Leaf A-D routes, and a PE that creates (S,G) state from Leaf A-D routes must originate a Source Active A-D route when the source is reachable over IP and the group is in the PIM-SM in ASM mode range.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiving router advertises a route towards the sender saying "send me this group", with a label of its own so the packets can be recognised, and a route target so the route only travels as far as it needs.

sections.title: Mixing Tunnel Types and Placing the Edges
sections.content:
For a given inter-area service P2MP LSP, the PE or ASBR at the root controls the type of the intra-area P-tunnel that carries the ingress area segment, but the type of the tunnel carrying the backbone area segment may be different from the types carrying the ingress and egress area segments. When it is desirable or necessary to use the same type of tunnel for the ingress and egress segments, the procedures on the ingress and egress ABR provide that. When an ingress ABR re-advertises a BGP MVPN I-PMSI, S-PMSI A-D route or a VPLS A-D route into the backbone area, it places the PMSI Tunnel attribute of the route into the ATTR_SET BGP attribute, adds that attribute to the re-advertised route, and then replaces the original PMSI Tunnel attribute with a new one, whose Tunnel Type may differ from the original. When an egress ABR re-advertises such a route into the egress area, if the route carries the ATTR_SET attribute, the ABR sets the Tunnel Type of the PMSI Tunnel attribute in the re-advertised route to the Tunnel Type carried in the ATTR_SET attribute, and removes the ATTR_SET from the route.

The procedures also allow the placement of ingress and egress PEs in the backbone area, the placement of egress PEs in the ingress area, and the placement of ingress PEs in the egress area. For instance, a global table multicast service might be provided in the ingress and egress areas over PIM-based IP/GRE P-tunnels while the data is carried through the backbone area over MPLS P-tunnels. That works if the ABR connecting the ingress area to the backbone follows the procedures for ingress PEs, and the ABR connecting the egress area to the backbone follows the procedures for egress PEs. If MVPN service is provided in the ingress and egress areas with the data carried in PIM-based IP/GRE P-tunnels, the same technique carries the data over the backbone in MPLS P-tunnels, with the PIM-based tunnels treated as global table multicasts and the ABRs providing the ingress and egress PE functionality.
sections.plainLanguage: The three segments do not have to be built the same way, and the edge routers do not have to be in the areas you would expect. The border routers can stand in for the edge routers where needed.

sections.title: Forwarding the Packets
sections.content:
When the procedures of the document are followed, ABRs are required to perform only MPLS switching. When an ABR receives an MPLS packet from an incoming intra-area segment, it forwards the packet, based on MPLS switching, on to another outgoing intra-area segment. If the outgoing segment is instantiated using a P2MP LSP and there is a one-to-one mapping between the segment and the P2MP LSP, the ABR MUST pop the incoming segment's label stack and push the label stack of the outgoing P2MP LSP. With a many-to-one mapping, the ABR MUST pop the incoming label stack and first push the upstream-assigned label corresponding to the outgoing segment, if one has been assigned, and then push the label stack of the outgoing P2MP LSP. If the outgoing segment uses ingress replication, the ABR pops the incoming label stack and replicates the packet once to each leaf ABR or PE of the outgoing segment, and the label stack of each copy MUST first include a downstream-assigned label assigned by the leaf, followed by the label stack of the P2P or MP2P LSP to the leaf.

An egress PE must first identify the inter-area P2MP segmented LSP from the incoming label stack, and then forward the packet using the application bound to that LSP. For MVPN, the FEC of an inter-area P2MP segmented LSP is at the granularity of the sender PE, and the unique label stack associated with each such FEC lets the egress PE determine the sender PE. For VPLS, the FEC carries the VE-ID, so the egress PE can perform MAC learning for packets received from a given VE-ID. For global table multicast, it is sufficient for the label stack to identify the sender upstream node; when P2MP LSPs are used this requires that penultimate hop popping MUST be turned off, and when ingress replication is used the egress PE knows the incoming downstream-assigned label to which it has bound a particular (S/*,G) and must accept packets with only that label.

An ingress PE performs application-specific forwarding to identify the outgoing intra-area segment. With a P2MP LSP and a one-to-one mapping it encapsulates the packet in that LSP's label stack; with a many-to-one mapping it first pushes the upstream-assigned label for the segment, if assigned. With ingress replication it replicates the packet once to each leaf ABR or PE, with a downstream-assigned label first in each copy. Transit routers in each area perform only MPLS switching.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing special happens in the middle: the border routers swap one label stack for another, and the routers in between just switch labels.

sections.title: Registrations and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document defines a new BGP Extended Community called Inter-Area P2MP Segmented Next-Hop, which may be either a Transitive IPv4-Address-Specific or a Transitive IPv6-Address-Specific Extended Community. IANA has assigned the value 0x12 in the Transitive IPv4-Address-Specific Extended Community Sub-Types registry and the value 0x0012 in the Transitive IPv6-Address-Specific Extended Community Types registry, with this document as the reference for both code points. IANA has also assigned the value 0x08 in the PMSI Tunnel Types registry as Transport Tunnel. The document makes use of a Route Distinguisher whose value is all ones, so the two-octet type field has the value 65535, which IANA has assigned in the Route Distinguisher Type Field registry as For Use Only in Certain Leaf A-D Routes.

On security, the procedures described are subject to security threats similar to those experienced by any MPLS deployment. It is recommended that the baseline security measures described in "Security Framework for MPLS and GMPLS Networks" (RFC 5920), in the mLDP specification RFC 6388, and in the P2MP RSVP-TE specification RFC 3209 be considered. The security considerations of RFC 6513 are also applicable.
sections.plainLanguage: The new numbers are registered with IANA, and the same security precautions as any other MPLS network apply.
